Doest
DOO-est
v. (2nd pers. sing.)
The second-person singular present of do, with the Old English -est ending. Webster 1828 records it as the form used with thou, distinguishing it from the third-person doeth. Matthew 6:3 sets the two side by side in a single sentence.

Biblical Definition

Doest is what a man is asked about when God addresses him singly, and Scripture uses it to press the question of conduct onto one conscience at a time. The Lord attributes the form to God Himself in the psalmist’s praise: Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes (Psalm 119:68) — goodness of nature and goodness of action joined, so that what God does may be trusted because of what God is. Christ uses the form to govern the whole practice of almsgiving: But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth (Matthew 6:3). The singular is essential; giving is examined man by man, and the second half of the verse deliberately shifts to the third person doeth to make the point that even the giver’s own reckoning of his generosity is to be kept quiet. Elihu presses the question of whether human sin can touch God: If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him? (Job 35:6) — not that sin is trivial but that it injures the sinner, not the Almighty. Nicodemus grants what the miracles prove: no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him (John 3:2). And Ecclesiastes shows the form used of an absolute earthly power: who may say unto him, What doest thou? (Ecclesiastes 8:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives DOEST as the second person singular of the verb do, used with thou: to perform, to execute, to practise, to bring to pass. Webster notes the distinction between doest (second person) and doeth (third person), both of which the Authorized Version observes exactly.

expand to see more

DOEST — the second person singular, present tense, of the verb DO; used with the pronoun thou.

DO, v.t. — To perform; to execute; to carry into effect; to bring to pass.

To practise or commit, as an act, whether good or evil; as, to do justice, to do wrong.

To finish; to complete; whence the participle done, signifying finished or ended.

From Saxon don, to do — distinguished from doeth, the third person singular, which the Authorized Version keeps distinct throughout.

Key Scripture

Psalm 119:68 — "Thou art good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes."

Matthew 6:3 — "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth:"

Job 35:6 — "If thou sinnest, what doest thou against him? or if thy transgressions be multiplied, what doest thou unto him?"

John 3:2 — "The same came to Jesus by night, and said unto him, Rabbi, we know that thou art a teacher come from God: for no man can do these miracles that thou doest, except God be with him."

Ecclesiastes 8:4 — "Where the word of a king is, there is power: and who may say unto him, What doest thou?"

Modern Corruption

Matthew 6:3 forbids the publicising of one’s own giving, and the modern practice of named donor tiers, publicised pledges, and ministry generosity campaigns runs against the plain sense of a command the Lord gave in the singular.

expand to see more

The Lord’s instruction is stricter than the way it is usually softened. He does not say give without boasting; He says let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth, which forbids even the giver’s settled internal accounting of his own generosity, and He grounds it on the Father seeing in secret. Against that, the donor wall, the named seat, the pledge card read aloud, and the campaign that publishes giving levels are not neutral fundraising mechanics; they are the reward taken in advance, which is exactly the transaction Christ describes in Matthew 6:2 with the word verily I say unto you, They have their reward. A church may keep the records its officers need without turning giving into a public league table.

Psalm 119:68 guards the other flank. Because God is good, what He does is good, and the psalmist draws the practical conclusion in the same breath: teach me thy statutes. The modern instinct runs the other way, judging God’s character by whether His providences appear good to us, so that a hard year becomes evidence against His goodness. Job 35:6 punctures the related conceit that our conduct alters God’s condition. Sin ruins the sinner and offends infinite majesty; it does not wound God as a man is wounded. Holding both verses together yields the Reformed instinct in practice: God’s goodness is the fixed point from which providence is read, not the variable that providence adjusts.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asah (H6213), to do, make, accomplish; paal (H6466), to work, to do; Greek poieo (G4160), to do, to make; prasso (G4238), to practise, to perform habitually.

expand to see more

Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do, to make; the commonest Old Testament verb of action, used of God’s creating and of man’s obeying.

Hebrew paal (H6466) — to work, to do; often of deliberate workmanship, and of the workers of iniquity.

Greek poieo (G4160) — to do, to make; when thou doest alms (Matthew 6:3) and these miracles that thou doest (John 3:2).

Greek prasso (G4238) — to practise, to do repeatedly; the verb of habitual conduct (Romans 1:32; John 3:20).

Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to work, to labour; work out your own salvation stands nearby in Philippians 2:12.

Usage

"Thou art good, and doest good (Psalm 119:68) — the acts follow the nature."

"When thou doest alms (Matthew 6:3) — giving examined one conscience at a time."

"What doest thou against him? (Job 35:6) — sin ruins the sinner, it does not injure God."
